method: Every operation is assumed to move exactly the chosen block size, so the throughput is the sustained IOPS multiplied by that block size in bytes: 10,000 IOPS of 4 KiB is 40,960,000 bytes per second. Decimal units divide by 1,000,000 for MB/s and binary units by 1,048,576 for MiB/s; the data per hour is bytes per second x 3600 in decimal GB, the data per day is bytes per second x 86400 in decimal TB, and the time to move 1 TiB is 1,099,511,627,776 bytes divided by the byte rate in hours. The time per I/O is one second divided by the IOPS and is shown in microseconds. Little's law gives the average number of requests in flight as the completion rate times the average latency, so the queue depth needed is IOPS x latency in seconds (2 at 10,000 IOPS and 0.2 ms); when a queue depth is supplied, the IOPS that depth can sustain at the same latency is depth / latency, the headroom is that figure minus the entered rate, the utilization is the entered rate divided by that maximum, and an entered rate equal to the maximum is treated as covered. IOPS accepts 0.001 to 100,000,000, latency 0.001 to 60,000 ms, and the optional queue depth a whole number from 1 to 65,536; the nine block sizes run from 512 bytes to 1 MiB, decimal commas are accepted and exponent notation is refused. All arithmetic is double precision. The figures describe a steady state and do not model bursts, read/write mixes, sequential versus random placement, RAID write penalties, controller caches, filesystem overhead, thin provisioning or network storage, and the page does not benchmark, read or modify any device. It runs entirely in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: Wikipedia, IOPS: the operation rate a storage device sustains and the block size each operation transfers together determine the byte throughput.
Wikipedia, Little's law: the long-run average number of items in a system equals the arrival rate multiplied by the average time each item spends there, which is the queue depth relation used here.
Linux kernel block-layer documentation: I/O requests are queued against a device queue with a bounded depth, so the queue depth and the per-request latency bound the achievable completion rate.
